content.title: About
content.content: Shrimp are crustaceans from the families Penaeidae and Crangonidae. Baked or broiled shrimp are cooked at high heat, preserving their delicate flavor while giving them a light golden crust.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Shrimp can live in both fresh and salt water, but most commercial varieties are marine.
They can change the color of their exoskeleton depending on environment and stress levels.
Shrimp are a major source of protein in many countries, especially across Asia.
Worldwide production exceeds 7 million tonnes per year.
Shrimp can swim backward by a rapid flick of their tail.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Shrimp provide about 20 g of high‑quality protein per 100 g, making them an excellent protein source.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: They contain less than 1 g of fat per 100 g while still delivering beneficial omega‑3 fatty acids.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for blood formation and nerve function; shrimp supply it in substantial amounts.

items.title: Rich in minerals
items.content: Shrimp are abundant in selenium, zinc, iron, and iodine, which support immunity and metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Astaxanthin, the pigment that gives shrimp their pink hue, acts as a powerful antioxidant protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to shrimp.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Shrimp contain about 150 mg of cholesterol per 100 g; people with high cholesterol should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: In certain regions shrimp can accumulate cadmium or mercury; choose products from reputable sources.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Improper storage or insufficient cooking can allow bacterial growth leading to food poisoning.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Baked or broiled shrimp can be served as a snack, tossed into salads, pasta, rice dishes, or sandwiches. They cook quickly on a grill, in the oven, or on a skillet with a little oil and seasoning.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh shrimp should be kept in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C and used within 2 days. Frozen shrimp store up to 6 months at –18 °C. Thaw frozen shrimp in the fridge, not at room temperature, before cooking.
